readerTitle: The warehouse supervisor with a software idea
caseNote: 가상 사례 (물류창고 감독자의 도크 예약 소프트웨어 아이디어, 디자인 에이전시용 소프트웨어를 만들려는 개발자) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 사업용 소프트웨어 아이디어는 기능이 아니라 세 가지 질문으로 평가한다. 누가 지금 이 문제에 돈과 시간을 쓰는가, 그런 고객이 실제로 몇 곳인가, 나는 왜 이 시장에 맞는 사람인가.
misconception: 코드를 짤 수 있거나 시장 보고서 숫자가 크면 아이디어는 검증된 것이다.

sources.text: 이 유닛의 개념 레슨: 문제 먼저(ENT-01-03), 시장 규모 추정(ENT-01-04), 창업자-시장 적합성(ENT-01-06)
모든 인물, 회사, 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 인터뷰 결과(15곳 중 12곳이 문제라고 답함, 대형 2곳은 이미 시스템 보유)는 모두 가상 수치입니다. 실제 통계처럼 읽히지 않도록 카드에 illustrative 라벨이 붙어 있는지 확인하세요.
5번 카드의 '시장 보고서가 수십억 달러라고 한다'는 표현은 특정 보고서를 인용하지 않은 가상 대사입니다. 실제 수치를 넣지 마세요.

cards.title: The warehouse supervisor with a software idea
body: Every morning at 6 a.m., Maria watches trucks line up outside her warehouse. Some drivers wait two hours for a free loading dock. Others show up when the docks sit empty.
She sketches an app on a napkin: trucks book a dock slot, the warehouse sees the day's plan. It looks obvious. Is it a business?

image.label: Trucks queuing at warehouse loading docks at dawn
image.brief: 새벽 물류창고. 하역 도크 앞에 트럭 여러 대가 줄지어 대기하고, 몇몇 도크는 비어 있음. 앞쪽에 형광 조끼를 입은 여성 감독자가 냅킨에 앱 화면을 스케치. 트럭과 창고에 실제 회사 로고 없음.

cards.title: What should Maria do first?
body: Maria has a little savings and a cousin who builds websites. She wants to know if dock scheduling software is worth pursuing.

options.text: Pay her cousin to build a simple booking prototype
options.feedback: She gets something real to show, but she spends money before knowing whether other warehouses share the problem. This skips **problem before solution**.

options.text: Call 15 warehouse managers and ask how they schedule trucks today and what it costs them
options.feedback: **Problem before solution.** Asking about current habits and costs shows whether the pain is real and widespread, and it costs only her time.

options.text: Post an online survey asking if managers would like a dock booking app
options.feedback: Cheap and fast, but "would you like" invites polite yeses. Asking what people do and spend today tells her more.

cards.title: The pain is real, but not for everyone.
body: Twelve of the 15 managers said dock queues were a weekly headache. Most booked trucks by phone and a shared spreadsheet, and a clerk spent hours a day juggling calls.
Two large sites didn't care. Their warehouse systems already handled scheduling. Small sites with a few trucks a day were happy with the phone.
The problem lived in the middle: **mid-size warehouses** with enough trucks to create chaos but no big system to fix it. Maria's idea just got narrower and stronger.

cards.title: Count the customers you can actually reach.
body: Maria counts mid-size warehouses in her region and the next two. She guesses a price close to what a clerk's lost hours cost.
If only 1 in 10 buy at first, that's about **$120,000 a year**. A real starting point, not a fantasy.

breakdown.label: Mid-size warehouses
breakdown.detail: In her region and two neighbors

breakdown.label: If every one bought
breakdown.detail: The ceiling for this first market

cards.softwareNote: This is a bottom-up count: reachable customers × price. Software founders often skip it and quote a giant industry figure instead.

cards.title: Which number should she plan around?
body: A friend says, "Forget 400 warehouses. A market report says logistics software is worth billions. Grab 1% and you're rich."

options.text: The billions figure. It shows how big this could get
options.feedback: It sounds exciting, but it lumps in every kind of logistics software. **Sizing a market** means counting buyers who have your problem, not the whole industry.

options.text: Her 400-warehouse count, then expand region by region
options.feedback: **Sizing a market** bottom-up gives her a number she can test with real calls. If it works, the next region is another count, not a guess.

options.text: Neither. Sizing is guesswork, so just start selling
options.feedback: Selling early is good. But without a rough count, she can't tell whether 20 customers is a great start or most of the market.

cards.title: Why Maria, and not someone else?
body: **Founder-market fit** is how well a founder's experience, contacts and drive match the market they're entering.
Maria has lived this problem for years. She speaks the managers' language, and when she calls, they pick up. That insight and access are hard for an outsider to buy.
Her gap is building software. That gap is real, but she can fill it with a technical co-founder or a simple no-code tool. Filling the other gap, years of knowing the docks, is much slower.

cards.title: Now it's a software developer.
body: Sam is a skilled developer. He wants to build software that chases unpaid invoices for small design agencies. He has never worked in an agency and knows no agency owners.

options.text: Build it in a month. His coding speed is his edge
options.feedback: Fast building is a strength, but it doesn't tell him if agencies feel this pain or how they handle it now. That skips **problem before solution**.

options.text: Spend two weeks talking to agency owners, ideally teaming up with one who lives the problem
options.feedback: He tests the problem and closes his **founder-market fit** gap at once. An insider partner brings the trust and insight Sam lacks.

options.text: Pick a market where he already knows the users, like other developers
options.feedback: Stronger **founder-market fit**, but he drops an idea before testing it. Fit can sometimes be built through partners and time.

cards.title: Interest is not a sale.
body: Twelve managers saying "headache" is not twelve customers. People describe a pain far more easily than they pay to fix it. Maria's next test is a commitment: a paid pilot or a signed letter of intent.

Also, a first market of about $120,000 a year can support a good small business. It may not support a fast-growing startup that needs outside investors. Decide which one you're building before you judge the number.

image.label: A handshake turning into a signed pilot agreement
image.brief: 왼쪽에는 말풍선 "Yes, that's a pain!"이 여러 개, 오른쪽에는 서명된 계약서 한 장. 말풍선은 많지만 계약서는 하나라는 대비를 보여줌. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Judge a software idea by the problem, the count and the founder.
body: Before writing code, Maria checked three things from this unit:
list: **Problem before solution:** who struggles today, and what does it cost them?
**Sizing a market:** how many of those buyers can you actually reach?
**Founder-market fit:** why are you the right person, and what gap must you fill?
cards.callout: **Try it today:** take one idea you've had and answer these three questions in a single line each.
